curves-crossing-s3.title: Two changes in a town's bicycle market
curves-crossing-s3.text: A town graphs its market for bicycles with one downward curve D for buyers and one upward curve S for sellers. In April the town opens a network of bike lanes, and residents want more bicycles at every price. In July, long after the lanes opened, a fire at a parts factory means shops can offer fewer bicycles at every price.

items.q: Buyers want more umbrellas at every price after a rainy forecast. Shift the right curve and mark the new point where the curves cross.

why.correct: D shifts right along the upward curve S, so the new crossing E2 is higher and to the right: a higher price and a larger quantity.

key.because: a rainy forecast that makes buyers want more umbrellas

slips.S: The forecast changes what buyers want, so it moves D; sellers' costs have not changed.

items.q: A new machine lets bakers make bread more cheaply, so at every price they offer more loaves. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing.

why.correct: S shifts right down along D, so E2 is lower and to the right: a lower price and a larger quantity.

key.because: a machine that lowers bakers' costs

slips.D: The machine changes what bakers can offer, so it moves S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: On a market graph, what does the point where the two curves cross show?
options: The highest price buyers will pay for the good
The price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity offered
The lowest price sellers will accept for the good
The price at which buyers and sellers trade nothing

why.correct: At the crossing both curves give the same quantity at the same price, so buyers and sellers agree.
options: Buyers would pay more for the first few units; the crossing is where the curves meet.
Right: the two quantities match there.
Sellers would accept less for the first few units; the crossing is where the curves meet.
The crossing is where trade happens, not where it stops.

items.q: Which curve moved in the graph?
options: D shifted left
D shifted right
S shifted left
S shifted right

why.correct: The faded D1 sits to the right of the new curve, so D shifted left, and S did not move.
options: Right: the new D lies to the left of D1.
The new D is to the left of D1, not the right.
S has one position in the graph; it did not move.
S has one position in the graph; it did not move.

items.q: Compared with the first crossing, where is the new crossing in the graph?
options: At a higher price and a larger quantity
At a lower price and a larger quantity
At the same price and a smaller quantity
At a lower price and a smaller quantity

why.correct: D moved left down along the upward curve S, so the crossing moved down and to the left.
options: That would follow a shift of D to the right.
That would follow a shift of S to the right.
The price changes too, because S slopes upward.
Right: down and to the left along S.

items.q: Which event could have caused the change in the graph?
options: Sellers' costs for materials fall
More sellers enter the market
Buyers learn that a cheaper rival product works just as well
Buyers come to expect the price of the product to rise next month

why.correct: A cheaper alternative means fewer units wanted at every price: D shifts left.
options: Lower costs would move S, not D.
More sellers would move S, not D.
Right: buyers want fewer units at every price.
Expecting a higher price next month makes buyers want more now, shifting D right.

items.q: At which price in the table do the two curves cross?

why.correct: At \$20 buyers want 50 cases and sellers offer 50, the only row where the two quantities match.
options: At \$15 buyers want 60 but sellers offer only 40.
Right: 50 wanted and 50 offered.
At \$25 sellers offer 60 but buyers want only 40.
At \$10 buyers want 80 but sellers offer only 20.

items.q: Using the table, at a price of \$10, how many more cases do buyers want than sellers offer each week?

why.correct: At \$10 buyers want 80 and sellers offer 20: $80 - 20 = 60$ more cases wanted than offered.

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. The gap between them is the larger minus the smaller: 80 - 20.
That is the number buyers want. The question asks how many more they want than sellers offer: 80 - 20.

items.q: Sellers find a cheaper supplier, and at each price they now offer 20 more cases than in the table. At what price do the curves cross now?

why.correct: With 20 more offered, sellers offer 60 at \$15, which matches the 60 buyers want there.
options: Right: 60 wanted and 60 offered at \$15.
At \$20 sellers would now offer 70 but buyers want 50.
At \$25 sellers would now offer 80 but buyers want 40.
At \$10 sellers would now offer 40 but buyers want 80.

items.q: To compare two crossings on an exam graph, what should you show?
options: The new crossing by itself, since the old one no longer matters
The two curves alone, since the crossings are obvious from them
The new curve drawn over the old one, with no labels needed
Both crossings, labeled, with dashed lines to the old and new price and quantity

why.correct: Readers look for the old and the new equilibrium on each axis (P1 and P2, Q1 and Q2) so they can see the direction of each change.
options: Without the old crossing there is nothing to compare against.
Readers score marked and labeled points, not what seems obvious.
Unlabeled curves lose the labeling point.
Right: both points, both axes, labeled.

items.q: A frost ruins part of the coffee harvest, so at every price growers offer fewer beans. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing.

why.correct: S shifts left up along D, so E2 is higher and to the left: a higher price and a smaller quantity.

key.because: a frost that cuts what growers can offer

slips.D: The frost changes what growers can offer, so it moves S; what buyers want at each price has not changed.

items.q: A health report makes buyers want less soda at every price. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing.

why.correct: D shifts left down along S, so E2 is lower and to the left: a lower price and a smaller quantity.

key.because: a health report that makes buyers want less soda

slips.S: The report changes what buyers want, so it moves D; sellers' costs have not changed.

items.q: On a market graph, one curve shifts. The new crossing shows a lower price and a larger quantity than the old one. Which curve shifted, and which way?
options: D shifted right
D shifted left
S shifted right
S shifted left

why.correct: Price and quantity moved in opposite directions, so the crossing slid along D: S is the curve that moved. A lower price and a larger quantity mean it slid down D, so S shifted right.
options: A shift of D slides the crossing along S, so price and quantity would both rise.
A shift of D slides the crossing along S, so price and quantity would both fall.
Right: the crossing slid down along D to a lower price and a larger quantity.
S shifting left slides the crossing up along D: a higher price and a smaller quantity.

items.q: How does the crossing move in April?
options: Down and to the right along D: a lower price, a larger quantity
Up and to the right along S: a higher price, a larger quantity
Up and to the left along D: a higher price, a smaller quantity
Down and to the left along S: a lower price, a smaller quantity

why.correct: Residents want more bicycles at every price, so D shifts right. The crossing slides up along S: the price rises and the quantity rises.
options: That follows a shift of S to the right. The bike lanes change what buyers want, so D moves.
Right: D shifts right and the crossing slides up the upward curve S.
That follows a shift of S to the left, which is July's change.
That follows a shift of D to the left. Residents want more bicycles, not fewer.

items.q: Compared with just before the factory fire, how does the crossing move in July?
options: Up and to the left along D: a higher price, a smaller quantity
Up and to the right along S: a higher price, a larger quantity
Down and to the right along D: a lower price, a larger quantity
Down and to the left along S: a lower price, a smaller quantity

why.correct: Shops offer fewer bicycles at every price, so S shifts left. The crossing slides up along D: the price rises and the quantity falls.
options: Right: S shifts left and the crossing slides up the downward curve D.
That follows a shift of D to the right, which was April's change.
That follows a shift of S to the right. The fire means shops offer fewer bicycles.
That follows a shift of D to the left. The fire changes what sellers offer, so S moves.

items.q: In April the price and the quantity move the same way, but in July they move in opposite directions. Why?
options: April's change was larger than July's change
Buyers react to prices faster than sellers do
A second shift always reverses the first one
The crossing slides along the curve that stayed put

why.correct: A shift of D moves the crossing along the upward curve S, so price and quantity move together. A shift of S moves it along the downward curve D, so they move in opposite directions.
options: The size of a shift does not decide the directions. Which curve stayed put does.
Nothing in the scenario is about speed. The difference is which curve moved.
July's shift does not undo April's: the price rises both times.
Right: along S in April (both rise), along D in July (price up, quantity down).
